equities.name: S&P 500
equities.driverNote: ES=F closed 7200.00 on 24 November (from 7267.25, -0.93%) as the S&P 500 cash index fell 0.50% (-36.08) to 7,201.09, its eighth loss in nine sessions, giving back a tenth of Monday's 4.73% gain (CappNotes Closing Look, 24 November). The session was a rotation, not a liquidation: the Dow rose 0.85% (+423.39) to 50,018.70 - reported as its first close above 50,000, though one outlet says it had done so earlier in the year, a disagreement this ledger records rather than resolves since it does not score the Dow - while the Nasdaq Composite fell 1.48% (-356.03) to 23,733.54 and the Nasdaq-100 cash index 1.99% (-531.93) to 26,214.17. Breadth went the index's other way: 346 advancers to 154 decliners with nine of eleven sectors higher - Health Care +2.95%, Consumer Staples +1.66%, Real Estate +1.31%, Energy +0.97%, Financials +0.83% - against Industrials -0.53% and Technology -3.26%, and equal-weight RSP rose 0.54%, 104bp better than the cap-weighted index. The damage was concentrated in semiconductors: the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 7.88%, SOXX 8.27% and SOXL 24.55%, with Nvidia -5.86% a day after +31.48% and still about 35% below its 6 October record close, Micron -11.01% on a downgrade to Neutral and high-bandwidth-memory demand worries, Analog Devices -17.37%, Semtech -16.97%, MaxLinear -16.74% and Hewlett Packard Enterprise -16.31%. Retail reported well - Abercrombie & Fitch +19.69%, Kohl's +19.48%, Dick's Sporting Goods +14.59% - and Sanofi agreed to buy Insmed for $175 a share in cash, about $41 billion, the largest pharma deal in three years, taking INSM +14.13% and Sanofi's US shares +10.97% (CNBC and news log, 24 November). The macro print was the surprise of the day: Conference Board consumer confidence rose 11.4 points to 103.3 against a forecast near 92.2 from an upwardly revised 91.9, its highest since January 2025, with Richmond Fed manufacturing at 3 from -2 and Case-Shiller +2.1% y/y (Kitco, 24 November). The VIX barely moved, -0.98% to 26.36. Treasuries firmed slightly - the 2-year unchanged at 4.63%, the 10-year about 1bp lower at 4.90%, the 30-year flat at 5.29% and 2s10s about 27bp from 29bp - and a $70 billion 5-year auction cleared at a 4.719% high yield with a 2.37x bid-to-cover against a 2.31x average and a 0.3bp tail, though indirect demand was reported as the weakest since March 2020. Credit tightened for the first time in this document's recent window: high-yield spreads 356bp, -11bp, and investment grade 94bp, -2bp. WTI reversed Monday's slide, +2.35% to $82.05, with natural gas +15.30%, while gold fell 2.64%, silver 5.65%, copper 2.53% and bitcoin 2.20%. RSI 39.32, with the close 5.9% below the 50-day (7648.08) and 2.4% below the 200-day (7380.24); 1H structure choppy, weekly structure uptrend.

The sourcing, stated in full because this is the first non-zero crowd value in the ledger: Tickmill's 'Institutional Insights: Goldman Sachs Flows & Positioning Update 23/11/26' (by Patrick Munnelly, added 23/11/2026), summarising a Goldman Sachs multi-asset sales briefing, itself names fundamental long/short net leverage at the 5th percentile of one year and the 3rd percentile of three years, beta-adjusted net exposure at the 1st percentile of three years, CTA positioning in the Nasdaq-100 'near the bottom of its 10-year range', single-stock shorting as the 'largest weekly shorting flow since June 2022' and third largest of the decade, CTAs having sold about $57 billion of US equities over the past month to a net short, a Goldman Panic Index of 9.8 out of 10 with readings above 9.5 having historically signalled near-term relief, and S&P 500 futures top-of-book depth of about $4 million near year-to-date lows. The two accounts disagree on the exact percentile for net leverage - 1st versus 5th of one year - and neither is Goldman's own publication, which is why crowd is set at -1 rather than the -2 the cap would allow. An earlier report dated 22 October put Goldman's prime-book short leverage at the 99th percentile of its five-year history; it is 22 sessions stale and is not what this value rests on.

The S&P 500's eighth loss in nine sessions, the Dow's 0.85% rise to 50,018.70, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index's 7.88% fall and the 104bp gap between equal-weight RSP's +0.54% and the cap-weighted index's -0.50% are return and breadth facts, not volatility or positioning extremes, so none of them feeds volRegime or crowd. dataNotes: Run timing: this cycle ran the morning of Wednesday 25 November 2026 on contracts drafted by the GitHub Actions fetch job from Tuesday 24 November's close, which had already landed when this session started - no wait was needed. Every figure used is dated at or before 2026-11-24. What was excluded, and it matters more than usual this session: the four news-log entries dated 25 November, which cover the 8:30am release of October PCE and the Q3 GDP second estimate - the single print every Macro calendar vote in this document is written around. Those votes describe the risk as it stood at Tuesday's close, with consensus figures taken from sources dated 23-24 November, and nothing from the actual release influenced a vote or a number. Also excluded: anything dated 25 November on the tariff proposal and chip rout that the 25 November news-log entries record.

The session was a rotation, not a liquidation, and that is the fact most of this document turns on. The S&P 500 fell 0.50% to 7,201.09 (ES=F -0.93%) for its eighth loss in nine sessions and the Nasdaq-100 cash index fell 1.99% (NQ=F -2.35%), while the Dow rose 0.85% to 50,018.70, the Russell 2000 rose 0.57%, equal-weight RSP rose 0.54%, breadth ran 346 advancers to 154 decliners and nine of eleven sectors were higher. The whole decline sat in one industry: the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index -7.88%, SOXX -8.27%, Technology the only sector below -1% at -3.26%. The VIX barely moved, -0.98% to 26.36, and credit tightened for the first time in this document's recent window - high-yield spreads 356bp (-11bp), investment grade 94bp (-2bp). That combination is why the S&P 500 resolves bullish at all three horizons on mostly non-price categories while the Nasdaq-100 resolves flat at one and five sessions.

This document carries the first non-zero volRegime-or-crowd value in the ledger's record: crowd is -1 for the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100, and 0 for the other four. The change is in the sourcing, not in judgment. Earlier boards set crowd to 0 because the Goldman desk figures then available carried no percentile; the figures now available do. Two independent reports of the same Goldman Sachs prime-brokerage briefing dated 23 November themselves name fundamental long/short net leverage of 42.3% at the 1st percentile of the past year on one account and the 5th percentile of one year and 3rd of three years on another, beta-adjusted net exposure at a 1st-percentile three-year reading described elsewhere as a five-year low, the largest weekly single-stock shorting flow since June 2022, and - for the Nasdaq-100 specifically - CTA positioning 'near the bottom of its 10-year range'. The value is set at -1 rather than the -2 the cap allows because the readings are one session old, reached through secondary reporting, and the two accounts disagree on the exact percentile. It changes no call in this document: the S&P 500's three cells are bullish and so read as opposing a negative stretch, and the Nasdaq-100's three resolve to flat or no-call, which the overlay leaves alone. It does change two reported stretch labels - the S&P 500 from neutral to stretched-down at -2, the Nasdaq-100 from stretched-down to extreme-down at -3 - and that is recorded here so the change is visible rather than silent.

Sigma inputs: one improved, two are still carried, and all three are documented in their sigmaSource fields with the direction of the error stated. The dollar's is dated on S for the first time in this ledger - EUR/USD one-month at-the-money implied volatility of 6.35% as of 24 November from FinanceFeeds' options tables - replacing the 6.10% 13 November reading the last three boards carried; the components are identical at either value, so the +4 does not rest on the switch. Every 10-session Fed path vote here is written on that basis, with a 25bp hike priced at about 94-96% across CME FedWatch, Polymarket and Kalshi on S - down from roughly 98% on Monday - and Kitco at about 95%. newsLog.event: US futures slip as Monday's record-setting Nvidia melt-up cools. Hewlett Packard Enterprise sinks on Q4 results while Dollar Tree jumps on a raised annual profit forecast; investors are still questioning whether AI infrastructure spending will earn its returns.

Markets now fully price a 25bp hike at the Dec 8-9 FOMC. A $70B five-year auction and November consumer confidence are due today, with October core PCE on Wednesday the last major print before the meeting.

newsLog.reaction: A rare combination: hawkish Fed talk with yields still drifting lower into supply, as duration buyers step in ahead of the auction. newsLog.event: Sanofi agreed to acquire respiratory-disease specialist Insmed for $175 a share in cash, about $41 billion, the largest pharma acquisition in three years. The deal brings Sanofi Brinsupri (brensocatib), Arikayce and the phase 3 TPIP program as it faces the loss of patent protection on its top-selling drug; Sanofi said its 2026 financial guidance is unaffected.
newsLog.numbers: $175/share cash, $41.0B / EUR37.6B total; ~46% premium to Insmed's Nov 18 close (the day before Bloomberg reported Sanofi was weighing a bid); INSM +14% premarket, Sanofi shares +4.7% to EUR89.38, a one-year high. Largest industry deal since Pfizer-Seagen ($43B, Dec 2023)
newsLog.reaction: Insmed rallied toward the offer and Sanofi rose on the strategic fix for its patent cliff; the size of the deal revives large-cap pharma M&A expectations and gives biotech a bid on an otherwise soft tape.
